subject: Chemistry
concept_tested: Distinguishing a compound from a homogeneous mixture using fixed composition and separability
stem: A colourless liquid boils at a single fixed temperature at constant pressure. On electrolysis it yields hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed 2 : 1 volume ratio, and the ratio is the same for every sample tested. The liquid is best classified as

options.B: a homogeneous mixture of hydrogen and oxygen

distractor_rationale.A: An element cannot be decomposed into two simpler substances, yet electrolysis yields both hydrogen and oxygen.
distractor_rationale.B: A mixture of the two gases would not be a liquid under ordinary conditions, and the proportions in a mixture could be varied at will, whereas the observed decomposition ratio is the same for every sample.
distractor_rationale.D: A heterogeneous mixture has visibly distinct phases and non uniform composition, neither of which is observed here.

solution: Two pieces of evidence are given and they carry different weight. A single sharp boiling point at constant pressure supports classification as a pure substance under the criteria used in the textbook, since most mixtures boil over a range. It is supporting evidence rather than proof, because certain constant boiling mixtures also boil at a fixed temperature. The decisive evidence is the decomposition ratio, which is fixed at 2 : 1 for every sample tested. A composition that is the same whatever the source is the defining property of a compound. Decomposition into two simpler substances also rules out an element. Taken together the liquid is a compound.
formula_principle: Chemical classification of matter. A compound has a fixed composition by mass, a sharp boiling point at constant pressure, and can be decomposed into simpler substances only by chemical means.
common_misconception: Reading the words hydrogen and oxygen in the stem and concluding mixture, without noticing that the two gases are products of decomposition rather than components physically present. A second error is treating a sharp boiling point on its own as conclusive proof of a compound.
